text: Chapter 2 walked you through all four rule types. This lesson introduces the object that packages all of that together for one subledger application, built inside a tool called the Accounting Methods Builder: the Application Accounting Definition, or AAD.

An AAD is a complete accounting configuration for one subledger application - Payables, Receivables, Fixed Assets. It gathers every journal entry rule set you've defined for that application's event classes into one coherent, nameable, versionable package. It's the object that sits at the "per subledger application" layer the accounting method points to.

Why package it this way? If rule sets floated around independently, assigning an accounting method would mean hand-picking dozens of separate rule sets every time. One AAD per application means the method only references one object per application, and the whole application's configuration can be copied and versioned as a unit - which matters a lot next lesson.

The tool where you actually build AADs, journal line rules, account rules, description rules, and supporting references is called the Accounting Methods Builder, or AMB. Everything conceptual from chapter two gets configured there in practice, and an AAD is the top-level object you produce for each subledger application.

Picture the Payables AAD for a company. It contains rule sets for the Invoices event class, the Payments event class, and the Prepayments event class, each built from journal line rules and account rules. All of it wraps into one named AAD - something like "Standard Payables Accounting." A separate AAD exists for Receivables, for Fixed Assets, and so on.

So remember: an AAD bundles every rule set for one subledger application into one named, versionable package - that's what the accounting method actually references. Up next, lesson eleven: copying and modifying seeded definitions, the safe way to customize what Oracle ships.
